title: Medical-expense hardship reaches turnout and targeted political participation in CES module extracts
source_unit: CES 2018 and 2020 public crisis-module Stata extracts in the Politics of Personal Crisis replication package

federal_attribution_flag_share_within_ha.unit: percent weighted flag share; multiple-response item

bad_luck_attribution_flag_share_within_h.unit: percent weighted flag share; multiple-response item

observations.method: Analyst-produced weighted descriptive contrasts from the public Stata module extract; crisis_medexp is the exposure, outcomes are validated turnout and past-year political acts, and teamweight is the supplied module weight.
observations.uncertainty: No reproduced design-based standard errors are claimed. A basic weighted logistic screening extension gives contact OR 1.694 (model-robust 95% interval 1.106–2.593); this is not a survey-design interval. The published paper models total crisis count rather than a standalone medical-expense coefficient; this is an exploratory same-respondent extension.
observations.subgroup: Rows reporting versus not reporting trouble affording medical expenses.
observations.counterinterpretation: Medical-expense hardship may proxy health, income, insurance insecurity, prior turnout, employment, or other crises; the contrast is not causal.

observations.method: Analyst-produced weighted descriptive contrasts from the public Stata module extract; crisis_medexp is the exposure, outcomes are validated turnout and past-year political acts, and teamweight is the supplied module weight.
observations.uncertainty: No reproduced design-based standard errors are claimed. A basic weighted logistic screening extension gives contact OR 1.799 (model-robust 95% interval 1.023–3.164) and sign OR 0.510 (0.268–0.971); these are not survey-design intervals. The medical-expense-crisis group has 152 unweighted rows; the published paper models total crisis count rather than a standalone medical-expense coefficient.
observations.subgroup: Rows reporting versus not reporting trouble affording medical expenses.
observations.counterinterpretation: The 2020 pattern may reflect pandemic-era context, other crises, health, income, insurance insecurity, prior turnout, ideology, or selection; attribution cells are sparse and targeted contact/protest is not proof of institutional remedy or legitimacy change.

related_sources.claim: Published study design and broader total-crisis-to-participation findings.
Public replication package, scripts, and crisis-module data files.

boundary: This record establishes a same-respondent descriptive acquisition layer from medical-expense hardship to political participation. It does not establish a causal medical-specific effect, a design-based confidence interval, a bill-to-remedy pathway, or a trust/legitimacy outcome. Attribution variables are present in the source files but are not analyzed here.
